metadata.title: A Lagrangian relaxation view of linear and semidefinite hierarchies

nodes.name: Polynomial optimization problem $\P$
nodes.statement: (global) semi-algebraic optimization and in particular LP- or semidefinite relaxations for the polynomial optimization problem: \begin{equation} \P:\quad f^*=\displaystyle\min_\x\:\{f(\x)\::\: \x\in\K\:\} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a polynomial $f$ over a basic semi-algebraic set $\K$, with optimal value $f^*$.

nodes.name: Hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations based on Putinar's certificate
nodes.statement: - {\it Semidefinite} relaxations based on Putinar's certificate of positivity on $\K$ \cite{Putinar93}, where the $d$-th convex relaxation of the hierarchy is a semidefinite program which solves the optimization problem \begin{equation} \gamma_d=\max_{t,\sigma_j}\:\{\,t\::\: f-t=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j\,g_j\}. \end{equation} The unknowns $\sigma_j$ are sums of squares polynomials with the degree bound constraint ${\rm degree}\,\sigma_jg_j\leq 2d$, $j=0,\ldots,m$, and the expression in (\ref{put-cert}) is a certificate of positivity on $\K$ for the polynomial $\x\mapsto f(\x)-t$.
nodes.statement_short: The $d$-th SDP relaxation maximizes $t$ subject to a Putinar SOS certificate for $f-t$ on $\K$.

nodes.name: Hierarchy of LP-relaxations based on Krivine-Stengle's certificate
nodes.statement: - {\it LP}-relaxations based on Krivine-Stengle's certificate of positivity on $\K$ \cite{Krivine64a,Stengle74}, where the $d$-th convex relaxation of the hierarchy is a linear program which solves the optimization problem \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{t\::\: f-t\right.&=&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left.\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\right\}, \end{eqnarray} where $\N^{2m}_{d}=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}:\sum_j\alpha_j+\beta_j\leq d\}$. The unknown are $t$ and the nonnegative scalars $\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$, and it is assumed that $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\K$ (possibly after scaling) and the family $\{g_i,1-g_i\}$ generates the algebra $\R[\x]$ of polynomials. Problem (\ref{kriv-cert}) is an LP because stating that the two polynomials in both sides of ``$=$" are equal yields linear constraints on the $\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$'s. For instance, the LP-hierarchy from Sherali-Adams' RLT \cite{SheraliAdams90} and their variants \cite{SheraliAdams99} are of this form.
nodes.statement_short: The $d$-th LP relaxation maximizes $t$ subject to a Krivine-Stengle representation of $f-t$ with nonnegative scalar multipliers.

nodes.name: Parametrized hierarchy of convex relaxations $\rho_d$
nodes.statement: Each relaxation in the hierarchy is a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem of the form: \begin{equation} \rho_d\,=\,\max_{\blambda}\:\{\:G_d(\lambda)\::\: \blambda\geq0\}, \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the concave function $G_d(\lambda)$ over the nonnegative orthant.

nodes.name: Equivalent problem $\tilde{\P}_d$ with redundant constraints
nodes.statement: consider the optimization problem $\tilde{\P}_d$ defined by: \begin{equation} \min_\x\:\{f(\x)\::\:g_j(\x)^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j(\x))^{\beta_j}\,\geq\,0,\: (\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}\}\end{equation} which has same value $f^*$ as $\P$ because $\tilde{\P}_d$ is just $\P$ with additional redundant constraints; and notice that $\tilde{\P}_1=\P$.
nodes.statement_short: $\P$ augmented with redundant product constraints $g_j^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\geq0$; same optimal value $f^*$.

nodes.name: Parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations $q^k_d$
nodes.statement: one may now impose on the same nonnegative polynomial $\x\mapsto L(\x,\lambda)-t$ to be a sum of squares (SOS) polynomial $\sigma$ of degree at most $2k$ (instead of being constant and equal to zero as in (\ref{lp-interpret})), and solve the resulting hierarchy of optimization problems: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rl} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\sigma}&t\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_d(\x,\lambda)-t=\sigma,\quad \forall \x\in\R^n\\ &\lambda\geq0,\quad\sigma\in\Sigma[\x]_k\end{array}, \end{equation} with $d=1,2,\ldots$, and parametrized by $k$, fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Relax the LP hierarchy by requiring $L_d(\x,\lambda)-t$ to be an SOS polynomial of degree $\le 2k$ instead of zero.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Semidefinite program form of $q^k_d$
nodes.statement: Then problem (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is the semidefinite program: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcll} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\Q}&t&&\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&\langle \B_\beta,\Q\rangle,\quad \forall \beta\in\N^n_{2k}\\ &L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&0,\quad\forall \beta\in\N^n_s,\:\vert\beta\vert>2k\\ &\lambda&\geq&0;\:\Q=\Q^T\succeq0, \end{array}\end{equation} where $\Q$ is a ${n+k\choose n}\times {n+k\choose n}$ real symmetric matrix.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit SDP form of $q^k_d$ with one PSD Gram matrix $\Q$ of fixed size ${n+k\choose n}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams' RLT linear program at step $d$
nodes.statement: Following the definition of the Sherali-Adams' RLT in \cite{SheraliAdams90}, the resulting linear program at step $d$ in the hierarchy reads: \[\theta_d=\displaystyle\max_{\lambda\geq0,t,h}\left \{ t\::\:f(\x)-t\,=\,\sum_{i=1}^nh_i(\x)\,x_i(1-x_i)\right.\] \[+\sum_{\ell=0}^m\:\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}}{ I\cap J=\emptyset; \vert I\cup J\vert \leq d}} \lambda^\ell_{IJ}\:g_\ell(\x)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j);\] \begin{equation} \left.h_i\in\R[\x]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\},\end{equation} where $\lambda$ is the nonnegative vector $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$. (If there are linear equality constraints $g_\ell(\x)=0$ the corresponding variables $\lambda^\ell_{IJ}$ are not required to be nonnegative.)
nodes.statement_short: The RLT linear program at level $d$: represent $f-t$ using $x_i(1-x_i)$ multipliers and products of at most $d$ literals with each $g_\ell$.

nodes.name: 0/1 analogue of the parametrized semidefinite hierarchy
nodes.statement: Hence the 0/1 analogue of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) reads \[q^k_d=\displaystyle\max_{\lambda\geq0,t,h}\left \{ t\::\:f(\x)-t\,=\,\sigma(\x)+\sum_{i=1}^nh_i(\x)\,x_i(1-x_i)\right.\] \[+\sum_{\ell=0}^m\:\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}}{ I\cap J=\emptyset; \vert I\cup J\vert \leq d}} \lambda^\ell_{IJ}\:g_\ell(\x)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j);\] \begin{equation} \left.\sigma\in\Sigma[\x]_{k};\quad h_i\in\R[\x]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: RLT program of Sherali-Adams strengthened by an additional SOS term $\sigma\in\Sigma[\x]_k$.

nodes.name: Extended Lagrangian relaxation $\omega_d$
nodes.statement: Indeed consider the hierarchy of optimization problems \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \omega_d\,:=\,\max_{\sigma_j}\:\{H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)&:& {\rm deg}(\sigma_j\,g_j)\leq 2d,\sigma_j\in\Sigma[\x]\\ &&j=1,\ldots,m\}, \end{eqnarray} $d\in\N$, where $\sigma\mapsto H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ is the function \[H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)\,:=\,\min_\x\:\{f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(\x)\,g_j(\x)\:\}.\] For each $d\in\N$, problem (\ref{ex-lagrangian}) is an obvious relaxation of $\P$ and in fact is an {\it extended Lagrangian relaxation} of $\P$ where the multipliers are now allowed to be SOS polynomials with a degree bound, instead of constant nonnegative polynomials (i.e., SOS polynomials of degree zero).
nodes.statement_short: Lagrangian relaxation of $\P$ in which the multipliers are degree-bounded SOS polynomials rather than nonnegative scalars.
nodes.section: On the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: 0/1 form of the equivalent problem $\tilde{\P}_d$
nodes.statement: In this context, the problem $\tilde{\P}_d$ equivalent to $\P$ and defined in (\ref{pbtildeP}) by adding redundant constraints formed with products of original ones, reads: \[\begin{array}{rl} \min\{f(\x)\::& \x^\alpha \,x_j(1-x_j)\,=\,0,\: j=1,\ldots,n;\:\alpha\in\N^n_{d-1};\\ &g_\ell(\x)\displaystyle\prod_{i\in I}x_j\displaystyle\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j)\geq0,\quad \ell=0,\ldots,m,\\ &I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\};\:I\cap J=\emptyset;\:\vert I\cup J\vert\leq d\}. \end{array}\]
nodes.statement_short: The redundant-constraint reformulation $\tilde{\P}_d$ written out for 0/1 programs.

nodes.name: Basic semi-algebraic set $\K$
nodes.statement: where $f\in\R[\x]$ is a polynomial and $\K\subset\R^n$ is the basic semi-algebraic set \begin{equation} \K\,=\,\{\,\x\in\R^n\::\: g_j(\x)\,\geq\,0,\quad j=1,\ldots,m\}, \end{equation} for some polynomials $g_j\in\R[\x]$, $j=1,\ldots,m$.

nodes.name: Truncated index set $\N^{2m}_{d}$
nodes.statement: where $\N^{2m}_{d}=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}:\sum_j\alpha_j+\beta_j\leq d\}$.

nodes.name: SOS-convex polynomial
nodes.statement: An SOS-convex polynomial is a convex polynomial whose Hessian factors as $L(\x)L(\x)^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$. For instance, separable convex polynomials are SOS-convex.
nodes.statement_short: A convex polynomial whose Hessian admits an SOS (Gram) factorization $L(\x)L(\x)^T$.
differentia: whose Hessian factors as $L(\x)L(\x)^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$

nodes.name: Concave function $G_d(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: where $G_d(\cdot)$ is the concave function defined by: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber G_d(\lambda)\,:=\,\min_\x\:\left\{f(\x)\right.&-&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}(\x)\right)\times\\ &&\left. \left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\x))^{\beta_j}\right)\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The dual (Lagrangian) function: unconstrained minimum over $\x$ of $f$ minus the $\lambda$-weighted products of $g_j$'s and $(1-g_j)$'s.

nodes.name: Lagrangian polynomial $L_d(\x,\lambda)$
nodes.statement: evaluating $G_d(\lambda)$ at a point $\lambda\geq0$ requires computing the unconstrained global minimum of the function \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \x\mapsto L_d(\x,\lambda)&:=& f(\x)-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\x)^{\alpha_j}\right) \times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\x))^{\beta_j}\right),\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The generalized Lagrangian $L_d(\x,\lambda)=f(\x)-\sum\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\prod g_j^{\alpha_j}\prod(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}$, whose global minimum is $G_d(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Space of polynomials of degree at most $d$, $\R[\x]_d$
nodes.statement: Denote by $\R[\x]_d\subset\R[\x]$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $d$, which forms a vector space of dimension $s(d)={n+d\choose d}$, with e.g., the usual canonical basis $(\x^\alpha)$ of monomials.

nodes.name: Space of sums of squares polynomials $\Sigma[\x]$
nodes.statement: Also, denote by $\Sigma[\x]\subset\R[\x]$ (resp. $\Sigma[\x]_d\subset\R[\x]_{2d}$) the space of sums of squares (s.o.s.) polynomials (resp. s.o.s. polynomials of degree at most $2d$).
nodes.genus: the space of sums of squares (s.o.s.) polynomials
differentia: s.o.s. polynomials of degree at most $2d$

nodes.name: Coefficient vector $\f$ of a polynomial
nodes.statement: If $f\in\R[\x]_d$, write $f(\x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\N^n_d}f_\alpha \x^\alpha$ in the canonical basis and denote by $\f=(f_\alpha)\in\R^{s(d)}$ its vector of coefficients.

nodes.name: Space of real symmetric matrices $\s^n$ and the notation $\A\succeq0$
nodes.statement: Finally, let $\s^n$ denote the space of $n\times n$ real symmetric matrices, with inner product $\la \A,\B\ra ={\rm trace}\,\A\B$, and where the notation $\A\succeq0$ (resp. $\A\succ0$) stands for $\A$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.genus: the space of $n\times n$ real symmetric matrices

nodes.name: Quadratic module $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$
nodes.statement: With $g_0:=1$, the quadratic module $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subset\R[\x]$ generated by polynomials $g_1,\ldots,g_m$, is defined by \[Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\,:=\,\{\sum_{j=0}^m\sigma_j\,g_j\::\:\sigma_j\in\Sigma[\x]\}.\]

nodes.name: Slater's condition
nodes.statement: Slater's condition holds for $\P$ if there exists $\x_0\in\K$ such that $g_j(\x_0)>0$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$.
differentia: there exists $\x_0\in\K$ such that $g_j(\x_0)>0$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$

nodes.name: Monomial basis vector $\v_k(\x)$
nodes.statement: Next, for $k\in\N$ such that $2k\leq s$, let $\v_k(\x)$ be the vector of the monomial basis $(\x^\beta)$, $\beta\in\N^n_k$, of $\R[\x]_k$
nodes.genus: the vector of the monomial basis $(\x^\beta)$

nodes.name: 0/1 program data $\K=\{\x:\A\x\leq\b\}\cap\{0,1\}^n$
nodes.statement: Consider 0/1 programs with $f\in\R[\x]$, and feasible set $\K=\{\x:\A\x\leq\b\}\cap\{0,1\}^n$, for some real matrix $\A\in\R^{m\times n}$ and some vector $\b\in\R^m$. The Sherali-Adams's RLT hierarchy \cite{SheraliAdams90} belongs to the family of LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) but with a more specific form since $\K\subset [0,1]^n$. Notice that the family $\{1,x_1,(1-x_1),\ldots,x_n,(1-x_n)\}$ generates the algebra $\R[\x]$. Let $g_\ell(\x)=(b-\A\x)_\ell$, $\ell=1,\ldots,m$, and $g_0(\x)=1$.
nodes.statement_short: The 0/1 setting: $\K$ is a polytope intersected with the hypercube, with $g_\ell=(b-\A\x)_\ell$ and $g_0=1$.
differentia: for some real matrix $\A\in\R^{m\times n}$ and some vector $\b\in\R^m$

nodes.name: Real variety $\V$ of active constraint products
nodes.statement: Next, define $\V\subset\R^n$ to be the real variety: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \left\{\x\in\R^n\right.&:& \left(\prod_{j\in J^1_{\alpha\beta}}g_j(\x)\right) \left(\prod_{j\in J^2_{\alpha\beta}}(1-g_j(\x))\right)\,=\,0,\\ &&\left.\forall\:(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: The variety where all products of active constraints indexed by $\Omega$ vanish.

nodes.name: Extended Lagrangian $L(\x,\sigma)$
nodes.statement: and like for the usual Lagrangian, minimizing the extended Lagrangian \[\x\mapsto L(\x,\sigma):=f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(\x)\,g_j(\x),\] is in general an NP-hard problem.
nodes.statement_short: The Lagrangian with SOS multipliers $\sigma_j$ in place of nonnegative scalars.
nodes.section: On the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Extended dual function $H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$
nodes.statement: where $\sigma\mapsto H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ is the function \[H(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)\,:=\,\min_\x\:\{f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(\x)\,g_j(\x)\:\}.\]
nodes.section: On the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Assumption 1
nodes.statement: $\K$ is compact and $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\K$ for all $j=1,\ldots,m$. Moreover, the family of polynomials $\{g_j, 1-g_j\}$ generates the algebra $\R[\x]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\K$ compact, $0\le g_j\le1$ on $\K$, and $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ generates $\R[\x]$.

nodes.name: LP-relaxation rewritten via the Lagrangian polynomial
nodes.statement: Observe that the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) can be written \begin{equation} \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{\:t\::\: L_d(\x,\lambda)-t\,=\,0,\quad \forall \x\in\R^n\:\right\}, \end{equation} where $L_d$ has been defined in (\ref{functionL}).
nodes.statement_short: $\theta_d$ maximizes $t$ subject to $L_d(\x,\lambda)-t$ being identically zero.

nodes.name: Coefficient expansion of $L_d(\x,\lambda)-t$
nodes.statement: \[\x\mapsto L_d(\x,\lambda)-t\,:=\,\sum_{\beta\in\N^n_s}L_\beta(\lambda,t)\,\x^\beta,\] where $s=d\max_j[{\rm deg}\,g_j]$ and $L_\beta(\lambda,t)$ is linear in $(\lambda,t)$ for each $\beta\in\N^n_s$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $L_d-t$ in the monomial basis; each coefficient $L_\beta(\lambda,t)$ is linear in $(\lambda,t)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Monomial-matrix expansion $\v_k(\x)\v_k(\x)^T$
nodes.statement: \[\v_k(\x)\,\v_k(\x)^T\,=\,\sum_{\beta\in\N^n_{2k}}\x^\beta\,\B_\beta,\] for some appropriate real symmetric matrices $(\B_\beta)$, $\beta\in\N^n_{2k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the rank-one monomial matrix in the monomial basis with symmetric coefficient matrices $\B_\beta$.

nodes.name: Putinar's and Krivine-Stengle's positivity certificates
nodes.statement: Let $g_0=1$ and $\K$ in (\ref{setk}) be compact. (a) If the quadratic polynomial $\x\mapsto M-\Vert\x\Vert^2$ belongs to $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$ and if $f\in\R[\x]$ is strictly positive on $\K$ then $f\in Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$. (b) Assume that $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\K$ for every $j$, and the family $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ generates $\R[\x]$. If $f$ is strictly positive on $\K$ then \[f\,=\,\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\N^m}c_{\alpha\beta}\,\prod_{j}g_j^{\alpha_j}\,\prod_{\ell}(1-g_\ell)^{\beta_\ell},\] for some finitely many nonnegative scalars $(c_{\alpha\beta})$.
nodes.statement_short: Two representation theorems for polynomials strictly positive on a compact $\K$: a quadratic-module (Putinar) certificate and a product (Krivine-Stengle) certificate.

nodes.name: Monotone convergence of the hierarchy $(\rho_d)$
nodes.statement: Let $\K$ be as in (\ref{setk}), $f\in\R[\x]$, $d\in\N$, and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold. Consider problem (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) associated with $\P$ and with optimal value $\rho_d$. Then the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\N$, is monotone nondecreasing and $\rho_d\to f^*$ as $d\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption 1 the values $\rho_d$ increase monotonically to the global optimum $f^*$.

conclusions: Then the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\N$, is monotone nondecreasing and $\rho_d\to f^*$ as $d\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Finite convergence at the first relaxation for convex programs
nodes.statement: Let $\K$ be as in (\ref{setk}) and assume that $f$ and $-g_j$ are convex, $j=1,\ldots,m$. Moreover, assume that Slater's condition\footnote{Slater's condition holds for $\P$ if there exists $\x_0\in\K$ such that $g_j(\x_0)>0$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$.} holds and $f^*>-\infty$. Then the hierarchy of convex relaxations (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) has finite convergence at step $d=1$, i.e., $\rho_1=f^*$, and $\rho_1=G_1(\lambda^*)$ for some nonnegative $\lambda^*\in\R^m$.
nodes.statement_short: For convex problems satisfying Slater's condition, $\rho_1=f^*$ and the maximum is attained at some $\lambda^*\ge0$.

nodes.name: Exactness of the first semidefinite relaxation for (SOS-)convex problems
nodes.statement: With $\P$ as in (\ref{def-pb})-(\ref{setk}) let $f,-g_j$ be convex, $j=1,\ldots,m$, let Slater's condition hold and let $f^*>-\infty$. Then: (a) If $\max[{\rm deg}\,f,\:{\rm deg}\,g_j]\leq 2$ then $q^1_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k=1$, is exact. (a) If $\max[{\rm deg}\,f,\:{\rm deg}\,g_j]\leq 2k$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex, then $q^k_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k$, is exact.
nodes.statement_short: Convex quadratic problems are solved exactly by $q^1_1$, and SOS-convex problems of degree $\le 2k$ by $q^k_1$.

nodes.name: Lagrangian relaxation of $\tilde{\P}_d$ yields an arbitrarily tight lower bound
nodes.statement: Let $\K$ be as in (\ref{setk}), Assumption (\ref{ass1}) hold and let $\tilde{\P}_d$, $d\in\N$, be as in (\ref{pbtildeP}). Then for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists $d_\epsilon\in\N$ such that for every $d\geq d_\epsilon$, the Lagrangian relaxation of $\tilde{\P}_d$, yields a lower bound $f^*-\epsilon\leq \rho_d\leq f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Adding enough redundant product constraints makes the ordinary Lagrangian relaxation arbitrarily tight.
assumptions: Let $\K$ be as in (\ref{setk}), Assumption (\ref{ass1}) hold and let $\tilde{\P}_d$, $d\in\N$, be as in (\ref{pbtildeP}).

nodes.name: Obstruction to exactness of the semidefinite hierarchy
nodes.statement: Let $\P$ be as in (\ref{def-pb})-(\ref{setk}) and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold. Let $\x^*\in\K$ be a global minimizer and let $I_1(\x^*):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\,g_j(\x^*)=0\}$ and $I_2(\x^*):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\,(1-g_j(\x^*))=0\}$ be the set of active constraints at $\x^*$. Let $0\leq k\in\N$ be fixed. The level-$d$ semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact only if $f^*$ (resp. $\x^*\in\K$) is also the global optimum (resp. a global minimizer) for the problem \begin{equation} \min_\x\:\{f(\x)\::\: \x\in \V\},\end{equation} where $\V\subset\R^n$ (see (\ref{real-variety}) below) is a variety defined from some products of the polynomials $g_j$'s and $(1-g_j)$'s. And if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the variety $\V$.
nodes.statement_short: Exactness at level $d$ forces $f^*$ to be the global minimum of $f$ on a variety built from the active constraint products.

nodes.statement: For 0/1 programs with linear or quadratic objective function, and for every $k\geq1$, the first semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}), i.e., with $d=2$, is at least as powerful as that of the standard hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}). nodes.name: Gain of the controlled increase of complexity
nodes.statement: We prove that the gain by this (controlled) increase of complexity is precisely to permit finite convergence (and at the first step of the hierarchy) for a non trivial class of convex problems. For instance with $k=1$ the resulting hierarchy of semidefinite programs solves convex quadratic programs exactly at the first step of the hierarchy. And more generally, for $k>1$, the first relaxation is exact for SOS-convex\footnote{A SOS-convex polynomial is such that its Hessian matrix is SOS, i.e., factors as $L(\x)L(\x)^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$.} problems of degree at most $k$. On the other hand, we show that for non convex problems, exactness at some relaxation in the hierarchy still implies restrictive conditions.

nodes.name: Polytope case via Handelman's result
nodes.statement: If $\K$ is the (compact) polytope $\{\x: \a_j^T \x\leq 1,\,j=1,\ldots,m\}$ for some vectors $(\a_j)\subset\R^n$, then invoking a result by Handelman \cite{Handelman88}, one does not need the polynomials $\{1-g_j\}$ in the definition (\ref{functionL}) of $L_d$. So for instance, suppose that $I_1(\x^*)=\{\ell\}$ at a global minimizer $\x^*\in\K$. Then exactness at some step $d$ of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) imposes that $f^*$ should also be the global minimum of $f$ on the whole hyperplane $\V=\{\x: \a_\ell^T\x=1\}$; for non convex functions $f$, this is a serious restriction. Moreover, if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the hyperplane $\V$.
nodes.statement_short: For a polytope with one active facet at $\x^*$, exactness forces $f^*$ to be the minimum of $f$ over the whole facet hyperplane.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: We first prove that $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$ for all $d$, so that the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\N$, is monotone nondecreasing. Let $0\leq\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}$. Then $0\leq\tilde{\lambda}$ with $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ whenever $(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}$, and $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=0$ whenever $\vert\alpha+\beta\vert>d$, is such that $G_{d+1}(\tilde{\lambda})=G_{d}(\lambda)$ and so $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$. Next, let $\epsilon>0$ be fixed, arbitrary. The polynomial $f-f^*+\epsilon$ is positive on $\K$ and therefore, by \cite{Stengle74}, \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}, \[f-(f^*-\epsilon)\,=\,\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right),\] for some nonnegative vector of coefficients $\c^\epsilon=(c_{\alpha\beta}^\epsilon)$. Equivalently, \[f-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\,=\,(f^*-\epsilon).\] Letting \[d_\epsilon\,:=\,\max_{\alpha,\beta}\:\{\vert\alpha+\beta\vert\::\:c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}>0\},\] we obtain $f^*\geq G_{d_\epsilon}(\c^\epsilon)\,=\,f^*-\epsilon$. And so \[f^*\,\geq\,\max_\lambda\{G_{d_\epsilon}(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,\geq\,f^*-\epsilon.\] As $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the desired result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity by zero-padding the multipliers, then Krivine-Stengle representation of $f-f^*+\epsilon$ gives $\rho_{d_\epsilon}\geq f^*-\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: This follows from Theorem \ref{thmain} and the fact that computing $\rho_d$ is just solving the Lagrangian relaxation associated with $\tilde{\P}_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Theorem 2.1 together with the identification of $\rho_d$ as the Lagrangian relaxation value of $\tilde{\P}_d$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.3
nodes.statement: This is because the dual method applied to $\P$ (i.e. $\tilde{\P}_1$) converges, i.e., \begin{eqnarray*} f^*&=&\max_{\lambda\geq0}\:\left\{\min_\x\:\{f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\,g_j(\x)\}\right\}\\ &=&\max_\lambda\{G_1(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,=\,\rho_1.\end{eqnarray*} Next, let $\lambda^{(n)}$ be a maximizing sequence, i.e., $G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\to f^*$ as $n\to\infty$. Since Slater's condition holds (say at some $\x_0\in\K$), one has \[G_1(\lambda^{(0)})\,\leq\,G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\,\leq\,f(\x_0)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n)}_j\,g_j(\x_0),\] for all $n$, and so $\lambda^{(n)}_j\leq (f(\x_0)-G_1(\lambda^{(0)}))/g_j(\x_0)$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$, and all $n\geq1$. So there is a subsequence $(n_k)$, $k\in\N$, and $\lambda^*\in\R^m_+$, such that $\lambda^{(n_k)}\to\lambda^*\geq0$ as $k\to\infty$. Finally, let $\x\in\R^n$ be fixed, arbitrary. From \[G_1(\lambda^{(n_k)})\,\leq\,f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n_k)}_j\,g_j(\x),\qquad\forall\,k,\] letting $k\to\infty$ yields \[f^*\,\leq\,f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^*_j\,g_j(\x).\] As $\x\in\R^n$ was arbitrary, this proves $G_1(\lambda^*)\geq f^*$, which combined with $G_1(\lambda^*)\leq f^*$ yields the desired result $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong duality gives $\rho_1=f^*$; Slater's condition bounds a maximizing multiplier sequence, whose limit $\lambda^*$ attains the maximum.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th-final}, $\P$ has a minimizer $\x^*\in\K$ and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions hold at $(\x^*,\lambda^*)\in\K\times\R^m_+$ for some $\lambda^*\in\R^m_+$. And so if $k=1$, the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is a nonnegative quadratic polynomial and so an SOS $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\x]_1$. Therefore as $q^1_d\leq f^*$ for all $d$, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $k=d=1$, which proves (a). Next, if $k>1$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex then so is the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$. In addition, as $\nabla_\x L_1(\x^*,\lambda^*)=0$ and $L_1(\x^*,\lambda^*)-f^*=0$, the polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is SOS; see e.g. Helton and Nie \cite[Lemma 4.2]{nie-helton-survey}. Hence $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma^*$ for some $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\x]_k$, and again, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $d=1$, which proves (b).
nodes.statement_short: Use KKT multipliers to exhibit $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ as a feasible-hence-optimal triplet, since the Lagrangian gap polynomial is SOS in each case.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.2
nodes.statement: If (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact at level $d\in\N$, then \[L_d(\x,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma(\x),\qquad\forall \x\in\R^n,\] for some $\lambda^*\geq0$ and some $\sigma\in\Sigma[\x]_k$. Equivalently, \begin{eqnarray*} f(\x)-f^*\,=\,\sigma(\x)&+&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}}\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\x)^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\x))^{\beta_j}\right).\end{eqnarray*} Then evaluating at $\x=\x^*$ yields $\sigma(\x^*)=0$ and \[\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\,>0\,\Rightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{array}{l} \exists j\in I_1(\x^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\alpha_j>0,\:\mbox{or}\\ \exists j\in I_2(\x^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\beta_j>0.\end{array}\right.\] So let $\Omega\,:=\,\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}\::\:\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}>0\}$ and for every $(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega$ let \begin{eqnarray*} J^1_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\,\{j\in I_1(\x^*)\,:\,\alpha_j>0\},\\ J^2_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\{j\in I_2(\x^*)\,:\,\beta_j>0\}.\end{eqnarray*} Next, define $\V\subset\R^n$ to be the real variety: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \left\{\x\in\R^n\right.&:& \left(\prod_{j\in J^1_{\alpha\beta}}g_j(\x)\right) \left(\prod_{j\in J^2_{\alpha\beta}}(1-g_j(\x))\right)\,=\,0,\\ &&\left.\forall\:(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray} Then for every $\x\in\V$, one obtains $f(\x)-f^*=\sigma(\x)\geq0$, which means that $f^*$ is the global minimum of $f$ on $\V$. If $k=0$ then $\sigma$ is constant and equal to zero. And so $f(\x)-f^*=0$ for all $\x\in\V$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the exact representation at the minimizer $\x^*$ to force active-constraint support, then build the variety $\V$ on which $f-f^*=\sigma\geq0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.3
nodes.statement: (a) Exactness implies that the polynomial $\x\mapsto f(\x)-f^*$ has the representation described in (\ref{sherali-def}) for some polynomials $(h_i)\subset\R[\x]_{d-2}$ and some nonnegative scalars $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$. Evaluating both sides of (\ref{sherali-def}) at $\x=\x^*$ and using $g_\ell(\x^*)>0$ for all $\ell=0,\ldots,m$, yields \begin{equation} \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.\end{equation} Let $\V$ be as in Corollary \ref{sherali-exact} with $Q:=\{(I,J)\::\:\mbox{$\exists\,\ell$ s.t. }\lambda^\ell_{IJ}>0\}$. Then from the representation of $\x\mapsto f(\x)-f^*$ in (\ref{sherali-def}) we obtain $\f(\x)-f^*=0$ for all $\x\in\V$ and the result follows. For (b) a similar argument is valid but now using the representation of $f(\x)-f^*$ described in (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}). And so exactness yields (\ref{aux-sherali}) as well as $\sigma(\x^*)=0$. Next, for every $\x\in \V$ we now obtain $f(\x)-f^*=\sigma(\x)\geq0$ because $\sigma$ is SOS.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the RLT representation at the inactive-constraint optimum $\x^*$ to see which multipliers can be positive, then read off the vanishing set $\V$; part (b) adds the SOS term.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $(\rho_d)$
nodes.statement: We first prove that $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$ for all $d$, so that the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\N$, is monotone nondecreasing. Let $0\leq\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}$. Then $0\leq\tilde{\lambda}$ with $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ whenever $(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}$, and $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=0$ whenever $\vert\alpha+\beta\vert>d$, is such that $G_{d+1}(\tilde{\lambda})=G_{d}(\lambda)$ and so $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend a level-$d$ multiplier by zeros to a level-$(d+1)$ multiplier with the same value.

nodes.name: Krivine-Stengle representation of $f-f^*+\epsilon$
nodes.statement: Next, let $\epsilon>0$ be fixed, arbitrary. The polynomial $f-f^*+\epsilon$ is positive on $\K$ and therefore, by \cite{Stengle74}, \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}, \[f-(f^*-\epsilon)\,=\,\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right),\] for some nonnegative vector of coefficients $\c^\epsilon=(c_{\alpha\beta}^\epsilon)$. Equivalently, \[f-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\,=\,(f^*-\epsilon).\] Letting \[d_\epsilon\,:=\,\max_{\alpha,\beta}\:\{\vert\alpha+\beta\vert\::\:c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}>0\},\] we obtain $f^*\geq G_{d_\epsilon}(\c^\epsilon)\,=\,f^*-\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Krivine-Stengle certificate to the $\epsilon$-shifted objective and read the coefficients as feasible multipliers.

nodes.name: Conclude convergence
nodes.statement: And so \[f^*\,\geq\,\max_\lambda\{G_{d_\epsilon}(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,\geq\,f^*-\epsilon.\] As $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the desired result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $\rho_{d_\epsilon}$ between $f^*-\epsilon$ and $f^*$ and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

nodes.name: Strong duality gives $\rho_1=f^*$
nodes.statement: This is because the dual method applied to $\P$ (i.e. $\tilde{\P}_1$) converges, i.e., \begin{eqnarray*} f^*&=&\max_{\lambda\geq0}\:\left\{\min_\x\:\{f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\,g_j(\x)\}\right\}\\ &=&\max_\lambda\{G_1(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,=\,\rho_1.\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Invoke convergence of the dual method of multipliers for the convex problem $\P=\tilde{\P}_1$.

nodes.name: Slater's condition bounds a maximizing multiplier sequence
nodes.statement: Next, let $\lambda^{(n)}$ be a maximizing sequence, i.e., $G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\to f^*$ as $n\to\infty$. Since Slater's condition holds (say at some $\x_0\in\K$), one has \[G_1(\lambda^{(0)})\,\leq\,G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\,\leq\,f(\x_0)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n)}_j\,g_j(\x_0),\] for all $n$, and so $\lambda^{(n)}_j\leq (f(\x_0)-G_1(\lambda^{(0)}))/g_j(\x_0)$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$, and all $n\geq1$. So there is a subsequence $(n_k)$, $k\in\N$, and $\lambda^*\in\R^m_+$, such that $\lambda^{(n_k)}\to\lambda^*\geq0$ as $k\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Slater's point gives a uniform bound on the multipliers, hence a convergent subsequence with limit $\lambda^*$.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit and conclude $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$
nodes.statement: Finally, let $\x\in\R^n$ be fixed, arbitrary. From \[G_1(\lambda^{(n_k)})\,\leq\,f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n_k)}_j\,g_j(\x),\qquad\forall\,k,\] letting $k\to\infty$ yields \[f^*\,\leq\,f(\x)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^*_j\,g_j(\x).\] As $\x\in\R^n$ was arbitrary, this proves $G_1(\lambda^*)\geq f^*$, which combined with $G_1(\lambda^*)\leq f^*$ yields the desired result $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Take limits at arbitrary $\x$ to get $G_1(\lambda^*)\geq f^*$ and combine with the reverse inequality.

nodes.name: KKT conditions at a minimizer
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th-final}, $\P$ has a minimizer $\x^*\in\K$ and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions hold at $(\x^*,\lambda^*)\in\K\times\R^m_+$ for some $\lambda^*\in\R^m_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Set up: a minimizer exists and KKT multipliers $\lambda^*$ are available.

nodes.name: Case $k=1$: nonnegative quadratic is SOS
nodes.statement: And so if $k=1$, the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is a nonnegative quadratic polynomial and so an SOS $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\x]_1$. Therefore as $q^1_d\leq f^*$ for all $d$, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $k=d=1$, which proves (a).
nodes.statement_short: For $k=1$ the Lagrangian gap is a nonnegative quadratic, hence SOS, giving an optimal feasible triplet.

nodes.name: Case $k>1$: SOS-convexity via Helton-Nie
nodes.statement: Next, if $k>1$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex then so is the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$. In addition, as $\nabla_\x L_1(\x^*,\lambda^*)=0$ and $L_1(\x^*,\lambda^*)-f^*=0$, the polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is SOS; see e.g. Helton and Nie \cite[Lemma 4.2]{nie-helton-survey}. Hence $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma^*$ for some $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\x]_k$, and again, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $d=1$, which proves (b).
nodes.statement_short: For $k>1$ SOS-convexity plus a vanishing gradient makes the Lagrangian gap SOS by Helton-Nie.

nodes.name: Write the exactness representation
nodes.statement: If (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact at level $d\in\N$, then \[L_d(\x,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma(\x),\qquad\forall \x\in\R^n,\] for some $\lambda^*\geq0$ and some $\sigma\in\Sigma[\x]_k$. Equivalently, \begin{eqnarray*} f(\x)-f^*\,=\,\sigma(\x)&+&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}}\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\x)^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\x))^{\beta_j}\right).\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Translate exactness into an explicit identity for $f-f^*$ with an SOS term.

nodes.name: Evaluate at the minimizer $\x^*$
nodes.statement: Then evaluating at $\x=\x^*$ yields $\sigma(\x^*)=0$ and \[\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\,>0\,\Rightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{array}{l} \exists j\in I_1(\x^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\alpha_j>0,\:\mbox{or}\\ \exists j\in I_2(\x^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\beta_j>0.\end{array}\right.\]
nodes.statement_short: Evaluating at $\x^*$ forces every positive multiplier to involve an active constraint.

nodes.name: Define the support index sets
nodes.statement: So let $\Omega\,:=\,\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\N^{2m}_{d}\::\:\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}>0\}$ and for every $(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega$ let \begin{eqnarray*} J^1_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\,\{j\in I_1(\x^*)\,:\,\alpha_j>0\},\\ J^2_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\{j\in I_2(\x^*)\,:\,\beta_j>0\}.\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the support set $\Omega$ and the active index sets $J^1,J^2$.

nodes.name: Define the real variety $\V$
nodes.statement: Next, define $\V\subset\R^n$ to be the real variety: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \left\{\x\in\R^n\right.&:& \left(\prod_{j\in J^1_{\alpha\beta}}g_j(\x)\right) \left(\prod_{j\in J^2_{\alpha\beta}}(1-g_j(\x))\right)\,=\,0,\\ &&\left.\forall\:(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Construct the variety where all active-constraint products vanish.

nodes.name: Conclude minimality of $f^*$ on $\V$
nodes.statement: Then for every $\x\in\V$, one obtains $f(\x)-f^*=\sigma(\x)\geq0$, which means that $f^*$ is the global minimum of $f$ on $\V$. If $k=0$ then $\sigma$ is constant and equal to zero. And so $f(\x)-f^*=0$ for all $\x\in\V$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\V$ the identity reduces to $f-f^*=\sigma\geq0$, and $\sigma\equiv0$ when $k=0$.

nodes.name: Part (a): RLT representation of $f-f^*$
nodes.statement: (a) Exactness implies that the polynomial $\x\mapsto f(\x)-f^*$ has the representation described in (\ref{sherali-def}) for some polynomials $(h_i)\subset\R[\x]_{d-2}$ and some nonnegative scalars $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$.
nodes.statement_short: Exactness of RLT gives an explicit representation of $f-f^*$.

nodes.name: Part (a): evaluate at $\x^*$
nodes.statement: Evaluating both sides of (\ref{sherali-def}) at $\x=\x^*$ and using $g_\ell(\x^*)>0$ for all $\ell=0,\ldots,m$, yields \begin{equation} \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Since no constraint is active, positive multipliers must have vanishing literal products at $\x^*$.

nodes.name: Part (a): identify $\V$ and conclude
nodes.statement: Let $\V$ be as in Corollary \ref{sherali-exact} with $Q:=\{(I,J)\::\:\mbox{$\exists\,\ell$ s.t. }\lambda^\ell_{IJ}>0\}$. Then from the representation of $\x\mapsto f(\x)-f^*$ in (\ref{sherali-def}) we obtain $\f(\x)-f^*=0$ for all $\x\in\V$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Take $Q$ to be the support of the multipliers; then $f\equiv f^*$ on $\V$.

nodes.name: Part (b): the semidefinite analogue
nodes.statement: For (b) a similar argument is valid but now using the representation of $f(\x)-f^*$ described in (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}). And so exactness yields (\ref{aux-sherali}) as well as $\sigma(\x^*)=0$. Next, for every $\x\in \V$ we now obtain $f(\x)-f^*=\sigma(\x)\geq0$ because $\sigma$ is SOS.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the argument with the SOS term, obtaining $f-f^*=\sigma\geq0$ on $\V$.

nodes.name: Theoretical and practical drawbacks of the LP-relaxations
nodes.statement: However, on the other hand, the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) suffer from several serious theoretical and practical drawbacks. For instance, it has been shown in \cite{Lasserre02a,lasserre-imperial} that the LP-relaxations {\it cannot} be exact for most convex problems, i.e., the sequence of the associated optimal values converges to the global optimum only {\it asymptotically} and not in finitely many steps. Moreover, the LPs of the hierarchy are numerically ill-conditioned.
nodes.statement_short: LP-relaxations cannot be finitely exact for most convex problems and are ill-conditioned.

nodes.name: NP-hardness makes the hierarchy $\rho_d$ impractical
nodes.statement: an NP-hard problem in general. After all, in principle the goal of Lagrangian relaxation is to end up with a problem which is easier to solve than $\P$, and so, in this respect, the hierarchy (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) is {\it not} practical.

nodes.name: Rescaling to satisfy Assumption 1
nodes.statement: Notice that if $\K$ is compact and Assumption \ref{ass1} does not hold, one may always rescale the variables $x_i$ so as to have $\K\subset [0,1]^n$, and then add redundant constraints $0\leq x_i\leq 1$ for all $i=1,\ldots,m$. Then the family $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ (which includes $x_j$ and $1-x_j$ for all $j$) generates the algebra $\R[\x]$ and Assumption \ref{ass1} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Assumption 1 is no loss of generality: rescale into $[0,1]^n$ and add box constraints.

nodes.name: Rationale for adding redundant constraints
nodes.statement: So the interpretation of Corollary \ref{lagrangian} is that the Lagrangian relaxation technique in non convex optimization can provide a lower bound as close as desired to the global optimum $f^*$ provided that it is applied to an equivalent formulation of $\P$ that contains sufficiently many redundant constraints which are products of the original ones. It also provides a rigorous rationale for the well-known fact that adding redundant constraints helps solve $\P$. Indeed, even though the new problems $\tilde{\P}_d$, $d\in\N$, are all equivalent to $\P$, their Lagrangian relaxations are not equivalent to that of $\P$.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent formulations have inequivalent Lagrangian relaxations, which explains why redundant constraints help.

nodes.name: Failure of the analogous property for the LP-relaxations
nodes.statement: Observe that this does not hold for the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) where generically $\theta_d<f^*$ for every $d\in\N$; see e.g. \cite{Lasserre02a,lasserre-imperial}.

nodes.name: Difficulties in solving the hierarchy $\rho_d$
nodes.statement: Problem (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) is convex but in general the objective function $G_d$ is non differentiable. Moreover, another difficulty is the computation of $G_d(\lambda)$ for each $\lambda\geq0$ since $G_d(\lambda)$ is the global optimum of the possibly non convex function $(\x,\lambda)\mapsto L_d(\x,\lambda)$ defined in (\ref{functionL}). So one strategy is to replace (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) by a {\it simpler} convex problem (while preserving the convergence property) as follows.
nodes.statement_short: $G_d$ is non-differentiable and hard to evaluate, motivating a simpler convex surrogate.
nodes.section: 3 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Fixed LMI size independent of the rank $d$
nodes.statement: Moreover in the semidefinite program (\ref{sdp-k}), the semidefinite constraint $\Q\succeq0$ is concerned with a real symmetric ${n+k\choose n}\times {n+k\choose n}$ matrix, independently of the rank $d$ in the hierarchy. For instance if $k=1$ then $\sigma$ is a quadratic SOS and $\Q$ has size $(n+1)\times (n+1)$. In other words, even if the number of variables $\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ increases fast with $d$, the LMI constraint $\Q\succeq0$ has fixed size, in contrast with the semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}) where the size of the LMIs increases with $d$. And it is a well-known fact that crucial for solving semidefinite program is the size of the LMIs involved rather than the number of variables.
nodes.statement_short: The LMI has fixed size ${n+k\choose n}$ for all $d$, unlike Putinar's hierarchy whose LMI grows with $d$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams ignores products between the $g_\ell$'s
nodes.statement: So all products between the $g_\ell$'s are ignored (see the paragraph before Lemma 1 in \cite[p. 414]{SheraliAdams90}) even though they might help tighten the relaxations. In the literature the dual LP of (\ref{sherali-def}) is described rather than (\ref{sherali-def}) itself.

nodes.name: Negative integrality-gap results for Sherali-Adams + SDP
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for 0/1 problems and for the parameter value $k=1$, the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}) is what is called the {\it Sherali-Adams + SDP} hierarchy (basic SDP-relaxation + RLT hierarchy) in e.g. Benabas and Magen \cite{benabbas1} and Benabbas et al. \cite{benabbas2}; and in \cite{benabbas1,benabbas2} the authors show that any (constant) level $d$ of this hierarchy, viewed as a strengthening of the basic SDP-relaxation, does not make the integrality gap decrease.
nodes.statement_short: At $k=1$ the hierarchy is the known Sherali-Adams + SDP hierarchy, whose constant levels do not shrink the integrality gap.

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams + SDP as a level-$k=1$ strengthening of the LP-hierarchy
nodes.statement: In fact, and in view of our previous analysis, the ``Sherali-Adams + SDP" hierarchy should be viewed as a {\it (level $k=1$)}-strengthening of the basic Sherali-Adams' LP-hierarchy (\ref{sherali-def}) rather than a strengthening of the basic SDP relaxation.

nodes.name: Price to pay for the less brutal simplification
nodes.statement: Hence by simplifying (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) in a less brutal manner than in (\ref{kriv-cert}) one recovers a nice and highly desirable property for the resulting hierarchy. The price to pay is to pass from solving a hierarchy of LPs to solving hierarchy of semidefinite programs; however the increase in complexity is controlled by the parameter $k$ since the size of the LMI in the semidefinite program (\ref{sdp-k}) is $O(n^k)$, independently of the rank $d$ in the hierarchy.
nodes.statement_short: One trades LPs for SDPs, but with LMI size only $O(n^k)$ and independent of $d$.

nodes.name: Exactness imposes restrictive conditions
nodes.statement: Hence Corollary \ref{badnews} shows that exactness at some step $d$ of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) imposes rather restrictive conditions on problem $\P$. Namely, the global optimum $f^*$ (resp. the global minimizer $\x^*\in\K$) must also be the global optimum (resp. a global minimizer) of problem (\ref{pb-variety}). For instance, suppose that only one constraint, say $g_k(\x)\geq0$, is active at $\x^*$. Then $f^*$ (resp. $\x^*$) is also the global minimum (resp. a global minimizer) of $f$ on the variety $\{\x\,:\,g_k(\x)=0\}$. And if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the variety $\V$!
nodes.statement_short: With a single active constraint, exactness forces $f^*$ to be the minimum of $f$ on the whole zero set of that constraint.

nodes.name: The constraints $\A\x\leq\b$ play no role in $\V$
nodes.statement: The constraints $\A\x\leq\b$ play no explicit role in the definition of the set $\V$. Moreover, if $f$ discriminates all points of the hypercube $\{0,1\}^n$ then exactness of the Sherali-Adams' RLT implies that $\V$ must be the singleton $\{\x^*\}$.

nodes.name: Different spirit of the semidefinite hierarchy; no obstruction to exactness
nodes.statement: But the spirit is different from the LP-relaxations as there is no problem $\tilde{\P}_d$ obtained from $\P$ by adding finitely many redundant constraints and equivalent to $\P$. Instead of adding more and more redundant constraints and doing a standard Lagrangian relaxation to $\tilde{\P}_d$, one applies an extended Lagrangian relaxation to $\P$ with SOS multipliers of increasing degree (instead of nonnegative scalars). And in contrast to LP-relaxations, there is no obstruction to exactness (i.e., finite convergence). In fact, it is quite the opposite since as demonstrated recently in Nie \cite{nie2012}, finite convergence is generic!
nodes.statement_short: The SDP hierarchy raises multiplier degree rather than adding constraints, and has no exactness obstruction.
nodes.section: On the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations

nodes.name: Conclusion: LP-hierarchy as brute force simplification
nodes.statement: We have shown that the hierarchy of LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) has a rather surprising interpretation in terms of the Lagrangian relaxation applied to a problem $\tilde{\P}$ equivalent to $\P$ (but with redundant constraints formed with product of polynomials defining the original constraints of $\P$). Indeed it consists of the brute force simplification of imposing on a certain nonnegative polynomial to be the constant polynomial equal to zero, a very restrictive condition.
nodes.statement_short: Summary: the LP hierarchy is a Lagrangian relaxation of $\tilde{\P}$ with a nonnegative polynomial forced to zero.

nodes.name: Conclusion: the parametrized hierarchy as a compromise
nodes.statement: However, inspired by this interpretation, one has provided a systematic strategy to improve the LP-hierarchy by doing a much less brutal simplification. That is, one now imposes on the same nonnegative polynomial to be an SOS polynomial whose degree $k$ is fixed in advance and parametrizes the whole hierarchy. Each convex relaxation is now a semidefinite program but whose LMI constraint has fixed size $O(n^k)$. Hence, the resulting families of parametrized relaxations achieve a compromise between the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}) limited to problems of modest size and the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) that theoretically can handle problems of larger size but with a poor behavior when applied to convex problems.
nodes.statement_short: Summary: replacing the zero polynomial by a degree-$k$ SOS yields SDPs with $O(n^k)$ LMIs, a compromise between the two hierarchies.

nodes.name: The LP-relaxations were not originally defined as a simplification
nodes.statement: At first glance, such an a priori simple and naive brute force simplification might seem unreasonable (to say the least). But of course the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) where not defined this way. Initially, the Sherali-Adams' RLT hierarchy \cite{SheraliAdams90} was introduced for 0/1 programs and finite convergence was proved by using {\it ad hoc} arguments. But in fact, the rationale behind convergence of the more general LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) is the Krivine-Stengle positivity certificate \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}.
nodes.statement_short: Historically the RLT hierarchy came first with ad hoc proofs; Krivine-Stengle is the real reason for convergence.

nodes.name: Convergence is preserved but drawbacks remain
nodes.statement: However, even though this brute force simplification still preserves the convergence $\theta_d\to f^*$ thanks to \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}, we have already mentioned that it also implies serious theoretical (and practical) drawbacks for the resulting LP-relaxations (like slow asymptotic convergence for convex problems and numerical ill-conditioning).
